chief_complaint: fever, sore throat, generalized swollen lymph glands, and mononucleosis-like rash after exposure
hpi_details: 25M presenting 3 weeks after high-risk exposure with fever, pharyngitis, diffuse lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, and high HIV RNA viral load while antibody test is still indeterminate.
ideas: He thinks he caught mononucleosis or a bad case of strep throat after kissing someone at a party three weeks ago.
concerns: He is terrified that his symptoms might mean he contracted an incurable sexually transmitted infection that will permanently impact his health and future relationships.
expectations: He hopes to have his throat swabbed and get tested so he can be prescribed medication to ease his severe throat pain.

available_results.note: Pattern is consistent with acute HIV during the antibody window period

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Retroviral Syndrome (Primary HIV Infection) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Retroviral Syndrome (Primary HIV Infection) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming acute infection with HIV RNA testing (since antibody assays may still be negative in the window period) and initiating antiretroviral therapy immediately upon diagnosis regardless of CD4 count, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fever, sore throat, generalized swollen lymph glands, and mononucleosis-like rash after exposure

Key HPI features: 25M presenting 3 weeks after high-risk exposure with fever, pharyngitis, diffuse lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash, and high HIV RNA viral load while antibody test is still indeterminate.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.5C, HR 96, BP 118/74, RR 16. Diffuse non-tender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy; pharyngeal erythema without exudate; diffuse maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal extremities; mild hepatosplenomegaly. Bloods: HIV RNA viral load markedly elevated (>500,000 copies/mL); 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combo immunoassay reactive (p24 antigen positive) with an indeterminate/negative antibody differentiation assay, consistent with the acute 'window period'; CD4 count transiently reduced at 450 cells/uL; mild transaminitis; heterophile (Monospot) test and EBV serology negative.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Retroviral Syndrome (Primary HIV Infection).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Recent high-risk exposure with this symptom cluster — needs urgent HIV RNA testing, not just antibody testing.
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with quantitative HIV RNA PCR (viral load) — the primary test for acute HIV, since antibody-based assays can still be negative in the window period; repeat the 4th-generation Ag/Ab test and differentiation assay to document seroconversion

Initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) immediately upon diagnosis regardless of CD4 count, per 'rapid/same-day ART start' guidance, after sending baseline resistance genotype and routine labs (e.g., Bictegravir/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir alafenamide as a typical first-line regimen)

Counsel on the markedly elevated transmission risk during acute infection given very high viral loads; advise consistent condom use, offer partner notification, and discuss PrEP for HIV-negative partners
Screen for concurrent sexually transmitted infections (syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, hepatitis B/C) and link the patient to ongoing HIV primary care with an ID/HIV specialist
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for fever, sore throat, generalized swollen lymph glands, and mononucleosis-like rash after exposure
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for infectious_disease
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: The mononucleosis-like illness that occurs 2-4 weeks after HIV acquisition, with fever, pharyngitis, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and rash, at a time when the antibody test may still be negative but the viral load is very high.
red_flags: Recent high-risk exposure with this symptom cluster — needs urgent HIV RNA testing, not just antibody testing

must_ask.say: How many weeks ago was the exposure you're concerned about?
Do you have a sore throat, fever, and swollen glands all together?
Have you noticed a rash on your body?
Have you been tested for HIV before, and what was the result?
What are you most concerned this might be?

history.answer: I've had a fever and a terrible sore throat for about four days, and I noticed swollen lumps popping up around my neck and body.
The fever started about four days ago, and it has stayed high pretty much continuously since then.
At home it went up to around 38.5 degrees, and I've been having shaking chills and severe whole-body aches.
I took some acetaminophen yesterday; it brought the fever down slightly for a few hours, but then it spiked right back up.
My throat hurts badly whenever I swallow, but I don't have a cough, phlegm, or any shortness of breath.
No pain or burning when I urinate, no needing to pee more often, and no flank pain.
I have mild nausea and a poor appetite, but no vomiting, diarrhea, or stomach cramps.
I have a dull, generalized headache with the fever, but no severe throbbing headache, neck stiffness, or confusion.
A flat, red spotted rash broke out over my chest and belly two days ago. I haven't noticed any bug bites, black crusts, or sores.
My joints and muscles ache all over, but no specific joints are visibly red or swollen.
I have woken up drenched in sweat the past two nights, but I don't think I've lost weight.
I've noticed swollen, non-painful lumps in both sides of my neck, under my armpits, and in my groin over the last three days.
I haven't traveled overseas recently, haven't been hiking in the woods or grass, and haven't handled animals.
No one at my home or workplace has had a fever or similar symptoms.
I have never received chemotherapy, radiation, or taken steroid medications or immune suppressants.
I have no heart problems or artificial valves, and I haven't had any dental work or cleaning recently.
I haven't started any new prescription medications or over-the-counter supplements.
About three weeks ago, I had condomless sexual intercourse with a new partner.
I have never used injection drugs or shared needles.
That unprotected sexual encounter took place exactly three weeks ago, and my symptoms started about four days ago.
I had a routine HIV test about six months ago that came back negative, and I haven't been tested since then.

I hooked up with someone at a party a few weeks ago, so I thought I probably caught mono or a severe case of strep throat. I had unprotected sex recently, and I'm terrified that this might be an incurable sexually transmitted disease that will ruin my future.
I'm hoping you can swab my throat, run the necessary tests, and prescribe something to make this awful throat pain go away.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I've never had any surgical operations and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications or herbal products, only the acetaminophen I took yesterday for fever.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or materials like latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I drink alcohol socially on occasion, about one or two beers on weekends.
I work full-time in an office and live by myself in an apartment.
Both of my parents are alive and well, with no major hereditary or chronic diseases in my family.

exam.finding: Temperature 38.5 C, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 96 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Pharyngeal erythema without tonsillar exudate, swelling, or mucosal ulcerations.
Both tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray, with no erythema or middle ear effusion.
Multiple non-tender, mobile, rubbery lymph nodes palpable in both anterior and posterior cervical chains.
Multiple non-tender, mobile axillary lymph nodes palpable bilaterally; no breast masses or skin retraction.
Bilateral non-tender, mobile inguinal lymph nodes palpable; no femoral or inguinal hernia.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation, with no wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no heart murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Abdomen is soft and non-distended, with no focal tenderness, voluntary guarding, or rebound tenderness.
Mild hepatosplenomegaly palpable; liver edge and spleen tip are smooth, non-tender, and palpable just below the costal margins.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on gentle percussion bilaterally.
Diffuse, non-pruritic, erythematous maculopapular rash distributed across the trunk and proximal limbs; no petechiae or eschars.
Neck is supple with full passive flexion; negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
